title: Treatment of subacute aphasia through communicative-pragmatic interaction and singing in Groups
summary: Language networks of the brain are affected in around a third of strokes, compromising verbal communication in everyday life and affetcs quality of life  negatively. Reduced participation, loss of independence, and decreased self-determination are experienced as particularly stressful (Bose et al., 2009). Consequently, a third of aphasic patients suffer from depression in the first 10 years after stroke (Ayerbe et al., 2013). The ILAT concept promotes verbal communication within an interactive group setting in a playful manner.  In contrast to the deficit-orientated individual therapy, ILAT is based on strengthening residual communicative skills and the associated language networks. In chronic aphasic patients  (> 6 months poststroke), aplication of ILAT has already proven to be effective (Meinzer et al., 2005, 2007; Pulvermüller et al., 2001; Stahl et al., 2016, 2018). In the subacute phase after stroke, the effectiveness has less been tested. The aim of this study is to investigate whether the resource-oriented approach also improves communication skills and has an emotion-stabilising effect in subacute aphasic patients.

interventions.name:
inhouse standard therapy over 3 weeks
Application of disease-specific individual therapy (3-4 per week a’ 45 minutes)
Plus one group therapy per week (1 x 45 minutes ILAT)

ILAT (Intensive Language-Action Therapy) over 3 weeks
Application of disease-specific individual therapy (3-4 per week a’ 45 minutes)
Plus daily group therapy (5 x 45 minutes ILAT per week)

Singing group over 3 weeks
Application of disease-specific individual therapy (3-4 per week a’ 45 minutes)
Plus daily group therapy (5x 45 minutes singing in a group per week)

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
-	Ischemic or hemorrhagic left hemispheric stroke (confirmed by imaging)
-	subacute phase (<= 3 month) post stroke at inclusion
-	18 years or older
-	Presence of a aphasia defined by test performance in AAT 
-	must be able to be mobilised in a wheelchair
-	sufficient vigilance for study participation
-	patient should be able to understand the study (with appropriate explanation) and must be able to provide consent. If necessary, relatives or caregivers can be consulted to assist in the decision-making process. Otherwise (if the patient is unable to give consent), the patient's representative will authorise participation in the study.
Exclusion criteria:
- Relevant infectious diseases (requiring isolation) that pose an increased risk of infection for the other patients participating in the group therapy (e.g. COVID infection, MRSA in tracheal secretions) 
- History of severe alcoholism or drug abuse, severe psychiatric illnesses such as psychosis (if not in remission)
- Previous stroke or other CNS lesion
- Severe cognitive deficits (dementia)
- Participation in other language intervention studies
